finding: §3.3 makes two statements about an invalid effective review_converge_on value without saying which command surfaces the error, and the two statements collide on `tp config --resolved`: the field 'appears in tp config --resolved' (a display command that annotates each setting with {value, source}), yet 'the layer that wins resolution holding an unrecognized value ... is rejected as a usage error (exit 2)'. For an INVALID winning value, a tester cannot write a deterministic assertion for `tp config --resolved` — does it exit 2 with the hint, or exit 0 and display the invalid value with its source? Test 17 only pins that the invalid winning value 'is rejected as a usage error (exit 2)' but names no command, so two engineers will assert exit 2 on different commands (one on `tp review --status`, another on `tp config --resolved`, a third on `tp set --workflow`) and get contradictory results.
suggestion: State the exact set of commands that validate and reject an invalid winning value (e.g. every command that resolves the effective workflow value, including `tp config --resolved`), and resolve the `tp config --resolved` conflict explicitly: either it errors exit 2 on an invalid winning value, or it displays the raw value with source and defers the error to the consuming command. Pin the triggering command(s) in Test 17.

finding: Test 5's phrase 'a new round with at least one finding where every finding omitted severity' juxtaposes a singular existential ('at least one finding') with a universal ('where every finding omitted severity') on the same clause. The normative rule it is meant to exercise (§3.4/§4.1) is precise: the round-level fallback applies only 'when no finding in the round carries a severity at all', i.e. a MIXED round (some findings with severity, some without) uses the LIVE recompute and treats the severity-less findings as blocking (§4.1). Test 5's garbled wording admits a careless reading in which a round with only ONE severity-less finding (others carrying severity) exercises the persisted-flag fallback — the exact opposite of §4.1. A tester should not have to reverse-engineer §3.4 to write the assertion.
suggestion: Rephrase Test 5 to mirror §3.4/§4.1's exact predicate: 'a new round that has at least one finding, where NO finding carries a severity (all omitted it)'. This removes the existential/universal collision and makes the whole-round condition unambiguous.

finding: The round-8 rewrite of §3.4 scopes the severity-less not-clean rule to "a round with at least one *surviving* finding that carries no severity," which literally also matches mixed rounds (some findings carry a severity, at least one surviving finding does not). The unchanged §4.1 and test 19 both scope "the round-level legacy fallback (§3.4)" to "only when no finding in the round carries a severity at all." Since both use "applies only," the changed section now describes a strictly larger set than the two unchanged cross-references that point at it. The round-7 wording ("at least one finding but a severity on none of them") was scoped to wholly severity-less rounds and matched §4.1/test 19; the rewrite widened it. Behaviorally harmless (a mixed round is not-clean anyway via §4.1's per-finding missing-severity=blocking rule), but the scope phrasing now drifts from the sections that reference it.
suggestion: Restore the wholly-severity-less scoping so it matches §4.1 and test 19, e.g. "applies only to a wholly severity-less round that has at least one surviving finding" (or "a round where no finding carries a severity yet at least one finding survives"), keeping the record-time not-clean computation tied to the same "no finding carries a severity at all" condition §4.1 names for the round-level legacy fallback.
